sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No. The hero band (0–1280 × 60–250) has no picture of the linens or cookware the headline names. The only visual is the tilted blue SALE sticker (about x 1012–1226, y 111–198), and it says less than the subhead "Up to 40% off through Sunday" right beside it. So the visual adds nothing and the headline has nothing to show. The viewer never sees what is on sale or why it is worth having this weekend. The hero reads as a generic sale banner that could belong to any shop. Fix direction: give the hero a real image of the sale goods, such as a made bed or a laid table. Let the headline and image share one idea and let the image carry the "weekend" mood. Then the sale badge, if kept, becomes a small detail rather than the visual. Taste: the source entry for this line is off the approved list. Weight: major.
2. **Apart from the pictures, do the type, colors, and shapes share one mood and era, so the piece reads as one whole rather than a collage?** No. The page is quiet and of a piece: Inter at modest weights, warm beige hero (#EEEAE4-ish), soft pastel tiles, thin grey card borders, small radii. The SALE sticker breaks all of that. It is fully saturated electric blue, in a heavy wide display face, rotated about 3–4°, and it is the only saturated colour, the only diagonal and the only heavy type on the page. It reads as pasted in from a discount retailer, and it takes the first fixation away from the headline. That cheapens a brand ("Marlowe & Finch") that otherwise presents as calm and considered. Fix direction: have the sale signal speak the page's own language. For example, set "Up to 40% off" larger, or in an accent colour drawn from the warm palette, inside the hero type. Or keep a badge but square it up and give it the page's type and a related hue. Taste or common sense: both entries are off-list. Weight: major.
3. *(Off-checklist, copy that commits the viewer to a price.)* "Up to 40% off" sits directly above a "Popular this week" row priced $34 / $89 / $52 / $68. None of these prices shows a was-price or a discount marker, so it can be read two ways. Either these items are on sale and the prices are already reduced, or they are full price and the sale is somewhere else. A shopper who assumes the first may feel misled at checkout. The headline "Linens and cookware for the weekend" also reads at first as products *for use* on weekends rather than a weekend-only sale. Fix direction: show sale prices against the original on discounted items, or label the row as not part of the sale. Put "this weekend only" or similar into the headline itself. The hero also has no ask (no "Shop the sale" link), so the "Sale" nav item at top right (≈1202–1232, 28) is the only route in. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.** Four product cards share one repeated program: the same border, padding, image ratio, bold name and plain price, so the row scans as a set at a glance. The headings say what they hold. "Popular this week" names its row plainly, and the logo plus Kitchen/Bedroom/Garden nav make clear in one look that this is a homewares shop.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The product images are flat colour tiles with a pale rounded rectangle, which look like placeholders or images that did not load. Check in a live browser whether real product photos load there. Whether the empty band below the cards (y ≈ 582–800) is the end of the page or more content below the fold.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; one mood and era)

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No. Two elements fight for first place: the tilted blue SALE badge (about x 1012–1226, y 111–198) and the headline "Linens and cookware for the weekend" (about x 56–535, y 95–180). The badge is the only saturated colour on the page and the only tilted shape, so the eye goes there first. Then it jumps left to the larger headline, which takes over on size and darkness. Neither of them carries the offer. The facts that make someone act, "Up to 40% off through Sunday" (about x 56–320, y 197–217), are the smallest and lightest text in the hero, so they are read last. The viewer sees that something is on sale but has to look again to find how much and until when. The badge's word "SALE" also repeats the "Sale" nav link and tells the viewer nothing new. Why: with two elements at equal pull and no clear winner, the eye has no single place to start (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, on one dominant focal point). Fix: pick one dominant element and give it the offer. Either put "40% off" or "Up to 40% off, ends Sunday" inside the badge so the eye-catcher carries the message, or move the offer up into the headline and calm the badge down so it supports rather than competes. **Defect. Major.**
2. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. The "Marlowe & Finch" wordmark (about x 48–209, y 20–40, roughly 20px bold) and the "Popular this week" section heading (about x 48–239, y 284–305, roughly 22px bold) look nearly the same size and weight, in the same dark colour and at the same left edge. A wordmark and a section heading do different jobs, but here they read as one level, so the type scale looks chosen one size at a time instead of in clear steps. Product names (~16px bold) and nav links (~15px regular grey) are also close in size, but weight and colour separate them well enough. Measure the wordmark and the heading. Fix: give the section heading a clear step of its own, or set the wordmark apart by form (a logotype, a different weight or face), so each level has one obvious job (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, on distinct levels). **Convention. Minor.**

**What's working.**
- Below the hero, the levels are clean. In each card the product name is bold and the price is regular at a similar size, so the name leads and the price follows with no extra size. That is the right way to make a fine distinction: weight, not another size step.
- Headings differ from body text by weight as well as size (bold headline and section heading against regular subtitle and prices), so the levels hold up without relying on size alone.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 1 yes, 2 no (one element dominates; text levels distinct)

I read the entries for these lines in `references/art-direction.md` only. I skipped the matching entries in `references/layout.md` and `references/typography.md`, and the crop script could not run because Bash was blocked, so I worked from the whole image. All pixel sizes above are by eye, not measured.

sections.report:
Walk (Arrangement and space). I couldn't run the crop script because Bash is denied, so I worked from the whole 1280×800 image, which is one screen.

1. One grid: **no**. The hero text starts at x≈56, but the logo, "Popular this week" and the cards start at x=48.
2. Exact alignment or clearly off: **no**. The same 8 px near-miss.
3. Baselines across columns: yes.
4. Space inside groups smaller than between: **no**. "Popular this week" is about 34 px below the hero and about 38 px above the cards.
5. Boxes hold one group: yes.
6. No accidental groups: yes.
7. No overlap: yes.
8. Edge margins: yes.
9. White space gathered: yes.
10. Balance: yes.
11. Centring chosen: yes.
12. Proportion: yes.
13. Eye path: **no**. The tilted blue SALE badge at the far right of the hero pulls the eye to the edge first. The eye then has to double back left to the headline. The badge leads nowhere.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid? / Is every element either exactly aligned or clearly off, with no near-misses?**
   - **Where:** the hero headline and subline start at x≈56. The logo, the "Popular this week" heading and the first card's border all sit at x=48 above and below.
   - **What the viewer gets:** an 8 px step on the page's strongest left edge. It reads as a slip, not a choice. The left margin wobbles at exactly the point where the eye moves from the brand to the offer.
   - **Why:** convention (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*; Samara, *Making and Breaking the Grid*).
   - **Fix:** start the hero text at x=48 to match the rest. If it should be indented, indent it clearly, by about one gutter (24 px) or more.
   - Defect/convention, **minor**.
2. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?**
   - **Where:** "Popular this week" (y≈284–305) sits about 34 px below the end of the hero band (y=250) and about 38 px above the card row (y=343). It is slightly closer to the hero than to the cards it labels.
   - **What the viewer gets:** the heading floats between the two areas instead of belonging to the product row. The hero tint does separate the areas, so the cost is small.
   - **Why:** convention (proximity; Lupton, *Thinking with Type*; Refactoring UI).
   - **Fix:** roughly double the space above the heading and halve the space below it, about 16–20 px to the cards.
   - Convention, **minor**.
3. **Does the arrangement lead the eye from the first element through the rest, with no line, gaze, or pointing shape that leads it off the edge?**
   - **Where:** the SALE badge, about x 1012–1226 and y 112–198. It is tilted up to the right and is the only saturated colour on the page.
   - **What the viewer gets:** the badge takes the first fixation at the top-right edge and points further right and off the page. The eye then has to jump back about 450 px left to the headline and the "40% off through Sunday" line, and after that down to the cards. The path starts at the end and runs backwards. The badge also repeats "Sale" without the terms, so the first stop carries the least information.
   - **Why:** taste/common sense, by eye-path reasoning (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, on direction in composition).
   - **Fix:** move the badge into the reading path, next to or just after the headline. Or keep it on the right but tone it down so the headline is read first, and let the badge carry the "40%".
   - Taste, **major**: it decides what is read first on a sale page.

**What's working.**
- **Product row:** four equal cards share one 24 px gutter and span exactly the same 48–1232 width as the header. Image, name and price sit on shared baselines in every card, so the row scans as one even list.
- **Hero split:** text on the left and a single accent on the right balance the band without centring it. The large empty middle of the hero reads as deliberate space, not leftover gaps.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the page continues below the empty bottom 218 px (y 582–800). If the page really ends there, the lower third is dead space. Check at full length.
- How the four-card row and the hero badge reflow at narrower widths.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (one grid governs the page; aligned or clearly off; heading nearer its group; clear eye path).

I couldn't run the crop and entries scripts because Bash was denied, so the walk used the whole image and the entry titles named in the checklist. All pixel positions are measured by eye from the image.

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** The hero headline (about x 56–535, y 95–180) breaks as "Linens and cookware for / the weekend". This leaves "for" hanging at the end of line 1 and cuts the phrase "for the weekend" in two. The viewer reads "Linens and cookware for" as an unfinished thought, then has to join it to the second line, which slows the one line meant to be taken in at a glance. The source is Bringhurst, *Elements of Typographic Style* §2.4. The entry notes that breaks in headings are not confirmed in Bringhurst or Hochuli, so treat this as common sense, not a confirmed rule. Fix: break after "cookware", so the lines read "Linens and cookware / for the weekend". A manual break or a slightly narrower measure would do it. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **One family, clear steps.** Every piece of text is in one sans family, and the levels are clearly apart: the headline (about 40 px bold), the section heading and logo (about 20 px semibold), the product names (about 15 px bold) and the prices and nav (about 15 px regular). Names and prices are the same size and differ only in weight, which is how it should be done. Nothing reads as a near-miss size.
- **Readable everywhere.** All the text sits on flat colour, with dark text on beige and white, and white on solid blue in the badge. The SALE capitals are spaced far enough apart not to clot.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **SALE badge.** I can't tell from a still whether the tilted badge (about x 1012–1226, y 111–198) is live text or a picture of text. If it is an image, it needs alt text that says "Sale" (WCAG 1.4.5). Better still, make it real text rotated with CSS, so screen readers and translation tools get it.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries), 1 unsure (text is real type, not a picture of text: the SALE badge)

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do warm colors sit on what should come forward and cool ones on what should recede? No.** The one focal accent on the page is the SALE badge (about x 1012–1226, y 111–198), a cold, saturated electric blue set on the warm beige hero band (y 60–249). Everything else is warm or neutral: the oatmeal band, the beige tiles and the near-black text. The badge still draws the eye, through saturation and lightness, but it looks like a sticker from another brand. It cuts against the calm "linens and cookware" mood that the rest of the page sets up, and it is the one element that doesn't belong to the palette. Itten (*The Art of Color*, warm-cool contrast) says to put warm colour on the focal element and to keep temperature consistent within one surface family. The fix is to take the accent from the warm side of the brand: a terracotta, rust or deep warm red at the same strength and size. That would come forward with the palette rather than against it. If blue is a fixed brand colour, the fix is to bring it into the rest of the page (links, nav "Sale") so it reads as part of the brand and not a one-off. Convention, with a taste component. Weight: minor, because the badge already gets the attention it needs. What fixing it improves is coherence and brand feel, not whether the offer gets seen.

**What's working.**
- Restraint. There is one neutral range (white, oatmeal, pale grays, near-black text) and one saturated hue, kept to a small badge. The sale is the only strong colour on screen, so nothing competes with it for the eye.
- Value carries the structure. Dark text on light grounds and the full-width band edge mean the hero, section heading and card grid all still separate in grayscale. The pale tiles don't need hue to read as image areas.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The four card tiles (y 358–507) look like image placeholders: flat beige, blue-gray, lilac-gray and beige panels with a lighter rounded rectangle. If those are unloaded product photos, the real colour balance of the grid depends on the photography. Check in a live browser. If they are meant as final art, the cool blue-gray and lilac tiles next to the warm beige ones mix temperatures within one card family for no visible reason, and they should share one warm tint.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (warm forward, cool recede)

Walk (working notes)

First read: the eye goes first to the blue tilted SALE badge (around x 1012–1226, y 111–198). Next it goes to the headline, then to the row of four cards. Each card holds a flat tinted box with a pale rounded rectangle in its middle. Those boxes read as empty placeholders, not product photos. The image is about one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image.

Job (assumed): a home-goods shop's sale landing page. It should get shoppers to browse the products and click through.

Pictures:
- Every image shows its content, no placeholder box: **no**. All four product images (y 358–508, at x 63, 365, 667 and 969, each about 248 px wide) are tinted boxes with a blank rounded rectangle. No product is shown.
- Full quality: yes (there are no photos to degrade; the shapes are crisp).
- Crops intended: yes (nothing to crop).
- Subject apart from background: yes (the placeholder shape separates from its tint; there is no real subject).
- One rendering style and level of detail: yes (all four are identical placeholders).
- Photos share lighting, grade and crop: yes (no photos).
- Icons share stroke, caps and radius: yes (no icons).
- One viewpoint and light: yes (no scene).
- Texture quiet: yes (none).
- No fake depth: yes (the SALE badge is flat with at most a faint shadow, and the tilt reads as a deliberate sticker).
- Logo has clear space, undistorted, own colours: yes (the "Marlowe & Finch" wordmark at top left has ample room).
- Logo simple enough small and in one colour: yes (a plain wordmark).

The one `no` line has no catalog entry, so there is no entry to open.

**Section.** Pictures: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** No.
   - **Where:** all four product images in the "Popular this week" cards are empty placeholders. They are about 248×150 px each, at y 358–508 and x 63, 365, 667 and 969.
   - **What the viewer sees:** a flat beige, blue-grey or lilac box with a blank pale rounded rectangle centred in it.
   - **Why it matters:** on a shop page the product photo is what sells the item. A "Stoneware bowl set" or "Wool throw" for $34–$89 is chosen on looks. With nothing shown, the shopper can't judge any item, and the row reads as an unfinished template rather than a curated "popular this week" pick. That costs the page its main job of getting people to click through on the sale. The empty boxes also leave the SALE badge as the only image on the page.
   - **What would make it fine:** if these are images that hadn't loaded when the screenshot was taken, rather than the design, check the live page.
   - **Fix:** put a real photo of each product in each slot. Use a consistent treatment across the four: the same background, lighting and framing, so the set reads as one collection.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, judged as common sense (no catalog entry). Major.

**What's working.**
- The four image slots share one size, aspect ratio and inset within their cards. Real photos dropped in will line up cleanly as a set.
- The SALE badge is flat, simple and tilted on purpose. It reads at a glance as a sticker and doesn't fake depth.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I can't tell whether the product images failed to load or are placeholders by design. Check the live page.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (every image shows its content), 0 unsure.

sections.report:
I've finished the walk and read the entries, so this is the final report.

**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has nav links, a button-like SALE block and product cards.

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower? / Does every control look like what it does?** The only thing styled like a primary button is the saturated blue rounded "SALE" block on the right of the hero (about x 1012–1226, y 111–198). But it's tilted like a sticker, and its label just repeats the nav's "Sale", so it reads as half badge, half button. The viewer can't tell whether to click it. Meanwhile the headline and "Up to 40% off through Sunday." on the left have no ask at all, so the hero states an offer and gives no clear way into it. Primary versus secondary action (Material Design 3, "Buttons"; Apple HIG, "Buttons"): one view should have one dominant, obviously pressable action. Fix: decide what the block is. If it's the way in, make it a real button, upright, with words that name the action (for example "Shop the sale"), placed next to the offer. If it's decoration, move it off the button's job and add a real button under the subhead. **Defect, major.**
2. **Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products? / Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search?** The header (y 0–59) has only the wordmark and four category links. There's no cart, search or account, which shoppers expect at the top right of any store. A shopper who wants a specific item has no search, and nothing shows that a basket exists. Jakob's law (Nielsen, "Jakob's Law of Internet User Experience"); Nielsen heuristic 7, flexibility and efficiency of use. Fix: add search and a cart with an item count at the top right, and an account link if the store has accounts. If they were left out of this mockup on purpose, say so, because the page reads as unfinished without them. **Convention, major.**
3. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them?** The hero promises up to 40% off, but the four cards under "Popular this week" (y 343–581) show single plain prices ($34, $89, $52, $68) with no original price, discount or sale tag. A shopper who arrived for the sale can't tell whether any of these items are on sale, so they have to go hunting. This is common sense; the catalog entry for it (Tognazzini) is off the approved list. Fix: if these items are discounted, show the sale price next to the struck original. If not, put sale items in this row first, or label the row so it doesn't seem to answer the hero. **Defect, minor.**

**What's working.**
- The four product cards are a clean, conventional pattern: picture, bold name, price, same order in every card. They read as clickable items you can compare at a glance.
- The nav links are plain words in the shopper's own terms (Kitchen, Bedroom, Garden, Sale), evenly spaced and well apart, so each target is easy to tell from its neighbours.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Hover and focus states on the cards, nav links and the SALE block. This matters most for the SALE block, because a hover state would show whether it's clickable.
- Whether the header is sticky and covers focused content when scrolling.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 26 yes, 5 no (one primary action; controls look like what they do; shortcuts such as search; what the user needs next; platform conventions), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured)
